title: Holika Dahan: the boy in the fire
hookLine: the night before the colors: a boy who wouldn't stop saying the name, and the fire that couldn't burn him
carry: bhakti: prahlada held the name, and it held him

lines: A BOY WHO WALKED OUT OF THE FIRE.
cards: The well-known photos of Holi show people drenched in pink and green and yellow powder, laughing in the street. But that's the morning.
The night before, in towns and villages and temple courtyards, people gather around a great pile of wood and dried branches, sometimes with a figure set on top.
At the right moment, it's lit, and the flames go up into the full-moon sky. People walk around it, throw in grain and coconuts, and hold up stalks of fresh wheat to roast.
And somebody's grandmother tells the story, again, about a little boy who sat in a fire and walked out.

teach.h: A KING WHO THOUGHT HE COULDN'T DIE.
teach.b: It starts with a demon king, Hiranyakashipu.
After years of fierce austerity, he wins an extraordinary protection: he can't be killed by man or beast, by day or by night, indoors or outdoors, on the ground or in the air, by any weapon.
Believing himself unkillable, he orders everyone to worship him. Everyone does, except his own small son, Prahlada.
Asked what the best thing he's learned is, the boy answers: hearing about Vishnu, singing his names, remembering him.

The Bhagavata Purana says his father tries poison, elephants, snakes, a cliff; each time the boy is kept safe. Then comes the part told at Holi bonfires. The king's sister, Holika, is protected against fire.
She takes Prahlada onto her lap and sits in a blazing pyre. And the fire goes the other way. Holika burns.

teach.h: A SON WHO WOULDN'T STOP SAYING THE NAME.
teach.b: Prahlada walks out untouched, still saying the name.
Said plainly: the Bhagavata doesn't tell the Holika episode; it lives in other retellings and in the festival itself.

Soon after, Vishnu comes as Narasimha, half man, half lion, and ends the king's cruelty. Here's the teaching. Prahlada is bhakti's model devotee, and his answer begins the classic list of ways Hindus love God.
Saying the name is the simplest, and the story says it's a refuge no tyrant can take.
So the bonfire is Holika Dahan, the burning of Holika. People circle it, as on day one hundred thirty-four, toss in new grain, and call it good's victory over evil.

how: On the full-moon night before Holi, many Hindu communities light a bonfire for Holika Dahan, retelling the story of Prahlada, walking around the fire, offering grain and coconut, and roasting new wheat or barley; the colors are played the next morning.

o: a spring festival: a bonfire, then colors
a day of silence and fasting for Vishnu
a boat race held on the river in monsoon

s: Holi is only the colors in the morning
it begins the night before, with the Holika Dahan bonfire.
the Holika fire episode isn't in the Bhagavata Purana
the Bhagavata tells Prahlada and Narasimha; the Holika fire lives in other retellings and in the festival itself.
Prahlada's answer to his father became a well-known list of ways to love God
hearing about Vishnu, singing his names, remembering him: that's how the classic list of bhakti begins.

games.q: you're Prahlada. your aunt pulls you onto her lap and sits down in the middle of a blazing fire. what do you do?
games.why: he keeps saying the name. the fire goes the other way: Holika burns, and Prahlada walks out untouched.

practice: Picture the bonfire, the heat on your face, the full moon above. Name one thing you'd like to put on it, a grudge, a fear, a habit of cruelty, and watch it burn to ash. Then do what Prahlada did.
If you pray, say a name you love, Ram, Krishna, or Om Namo Narayanaya, once with each breath, even with all the noise around you. If you don't, hold one true thing you won't trade away.

wordCard.voice: Holi. The spring festival that begins the night before, with a bonfire for Prahlada, the boy the fire couldn't burn. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit/Hindi holikā: the aunt in the story, and the bonfire named for her, Holika Dahan.

carryVoice: Your line: bhakti. Prahlada held the name, and it held him. Tomorrow, the colors come out. That's day one hundred forty-one.
